unit_manager_teaching.prerequisite_note: Complete the earlier service recovery activity. Read these concepts, then run this different ungraded example before opening the full assignment.

concepts.title: Read a supplied service unit
concepts.text:
A unit file tells the service manager how a named unit works. [Unit] holds its description and dependencies. [Service] describes how its program starts. A target is a named group of units to start together. [Install] tells Enable which target link to create; it does not start a program. The repaired separate example contains:

[Unit]
Description=App for sketch
[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/sim/bin/sketch-app
[Install]
WantedBy=sketch.target

Type=simple starts a program intended to keep running. ExecStart selects the program. The supplied /sim/bin identifiers name fixed virtual programs here; they are not host executables. Change the wrong ExecStart line, then save, reload the manager, and stop/start the old running service.

concepts.title: Saved files, loaded definitions and running programs
concepts.text: Saving changes a supplied file. Run systemctl daemon-reload to make the service manager read saved unit definitions; this does not restart a running program. A program already running keeps its previous settings until you stop and start it. A previous passing check or old log entry does not prove the current work is correct.

concepts.title: Investigate before changing more files
concepts.text: Use systemctl cat sketch-app.service to inspect its saved backing text and systemctl status sketch-app.service for current status. Open Loaded definition and current inputs below the editor to see the saved and loaded unit text and the settings used by its current program. systemctl show sketch-app.service -p Requires,Wants,After lists the supported dependency properties. journalctl -u sketch-app.service -o cat shows retained virtual messages. These queries change nothing; old messages are history, not proof of current success.

concepts.title: Start, then inspect status and logs
concepts.text: Here, starting a service also lets the simulated program initialize. A successful start message can still be followed by a configuration failure; inspect status and logs. A simple service is intended to keep running. Its active label alone does not prove the application is ready.

concepts.title: Current service and the next session
concepts.text: A target is a named group of units to start together. The default selects the group for the next session. Enabling links a service to that group; it does not start the program now. Stop affects the running program without removing that link. The default chooses the next-session target. Check work also tests the next session in a separate copy, so that check cannot repair the current assignment.

The saved unit points to the wrong supplied program. Load the corrected source, then replace the old current execution. Use the individually explained actions, then inspect current and next-session outcomes. Virtual ports are values for this exercise; nothing listens on your computer.

scenarios.title: Make preparation a real prerequisite
scenarios.objective:
Archive needs archive-ready data from its supplied preparation job before its application can run at8181. Repair the preparation input, make the application request preparation as a required dependency, and make it wait until preparation finishes. Starting the units by hand in the right order is insufficient: the saved settings must work next session too. Keep preparation active after its successful one-shot job exits.

Keep the supplied application and observer configuration, observer document, target documents, links and selected default unchanged. Finish with the observer running at9101. Check that the running application uses the prepared data and that the next-session test works too.

scenarios.title: Hand over a multi-unit service without damaging its observer
scenarios.objective:
Replace the old publication service with publish-app.service at9443, using publish-v2 data from the successful preparation job. Repair the saved application input, make the application request and wait for preparation, load the definitions, and bring the replacement into service. Preparation must remain active after its successful one-shot job exits.

Stop publish-old.service and remove its link from publish-spare.target. Enable the new application for publish.target and select that target for the next session. The fresh session must start only the new target, preparation, application and observer.

Finish with the observer running at9103. Preserve its document and configuration, the old service document/configuration, both target documents and every other supplied install link. Check that the running application uses the new data and that the next-session test works; old prepared data or a default-target edit alone cannot complete the handover.

unit_manager_teaching.prerequisite_note: Complete the earlier service recovery activity. Read these concepts, then run this different ungraded example before opening the full assignment.

concepts.title: Saved files, loaded definitions and running programs
concepts.text: Saving changes a supplied file. Run systemctl daemon-reload to make the service manager read saved unit definitions; this does not restart a running program. A program already running keeps its previous settings until you stop and start it. A previous passing check or old log entry does not prove the current work is correct.

concepts.title: Investigate before changing more files
concepts.text: Use systemctl cat release-app.service to inspect its saved backing text and systemctl status release-app.service for current status. Open Loaded definition and current inputs below the editor to see the saved and loaded unit text and the settings used by its current program. systemctl show release-app.service -p Requires,Wants,After lists the supported dependency properties. journalctl -u release-app.service -o cat shows retained virtual messages. These queries change nothing; old messages are history, not proof of current success.

concepts.title: Request preparation and wait for it
concepts.text: A dependency requests another unit. Requires makes that request a strong requirement, but does not put it first. Add After on the application or Before on preparation to order both requested jobs. A one-shot service runs one job and then exits: Type=oneshot describes this. RemainAfterExit=yes keeps it active after success. Here that job supplies named data for the application.

concepts.title: Start, then inspect status and logs
concepts.text: Here, starting a service also lets the simulated program initialize. A successful start message can still be followed by a configuration failure; inspect status and logs. A simple service is intended to keep running. Its active label alone does not prove the application is ready.

concepts.title: Current service and the next session
concepts.text: A target is a named group of units to start together. The default selects the group for the next session. Enabling links a service to that group; it does not start the program now. Stop affects the running program without removing that link. The default chooses the next-session target. Check work also tests the next session in a separate copy, so that check cannot repair the current assignment.

unit_manager_teaching.example_description: Repair the separate release application at virtual port7304, then finish with its observer running at5204. Prepare example-ready-4, retire the old service/current link, enable the replacement and select release.target; keep every other link and the named preserved files. Use the individually explained actions, then inspect current and next-session outcomes. Virtual ports are values for this exercise; nothing listens on your computer.
